title: How David Reese Mini-Sermonized an Assignment's Instructions
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a guest example from teacher David T. Reese: a written mini-sermon embedded directly inside the instructions for a three-part writing assignment (a letter, annotated writing moves, and a reflective piece on how the letter was written). Rather than a separate speech, Reese's mini-sermon is woven into the assignment sheet itself, using Stuart's 'do the work, and do it with care' framing to explain why the reflective third part matters even though it feels strange to students. Reese leans on Cornel West's distinction between 'cheap schooling' (doing assignments because they're assigned) and 'deep education' (doing work with care because of its intrinsic value) to reframe the task as motivational rather than merely procedural, and closes with a Samuel Beckett quote about failing better to normalize struggle. Stuart presents the piece as a model of how assignment instructions themselves can double as a mini-sermon, showing students the why behind an assignment in the same breath as the what.
points: Reese demonstrates that a mini-sermon doesn't need to be a separate spoken moment — it can be embedded directly into written assignment instructions, doing double duty as both task explanation and motivation.

Cornel West's 'cheap schooling' versus 'deep education' distinction gives students vocabulary for the difference between doing an assignment because it was assigned and doing it because of its intrinsic value.
Explicitly naming a student's earlier admission that they didn't care about an assignment turns a moment of vulnerability into a teaching example of 'doing the work but not doing it with care.'
Closing with Beckett's 'Try again. Fail again. Fail better' normalizes struggle as an expected, even necessary, part of becoming a stronger writer rather than a sign of failure.
The self-referential move of admitting the mini-sermon itself 'took a considerable amount of time and a lot of edits' to write models the same care-in-effort message it's trying to teach.
quotes: Like my buddy Dave Stuart Jr. says, getting good at anything requires just two things: 1) Do the work, and 2) do it with care.
That right there is a perfect example of doing the work, but not doing it with care.

Cheap schooling looks like students doing assignments because they were assigned them. Deep education looks like students doing work with care because they are discovering the intrinsic value of intellectual and spiritual flourishing.
We have to TRY new ways of thinking and new ways of writing. And most important, we have to be willing to struggle and FAIL.
It took me a considerable amount of time and a lot of edits for me to write what you just read, but I think it's worth it.
The sooner you develop a paradigm that embraces getting better, you'll flourish as a student and as a person; and the best part is, that goodness might never, ever stop!
